page_hint: Ch 7 §8 (mini-case, closing paragraph); compare Ch 8 §3 'Scope' and Ch 17

page_hint: Ch 10, §3 Worked Example, 'Data Parallelism: Replicating, Then Syncing Gradients' (compare Ch 9 §3 Option A and Ch 10 TP subsection)
quoted_clause: so for $N=8$ the per-rank traffic is $1.75 \times 280 \approx 490$ GB and the sync time is $T_\text{ring} = 2\frac{N-1}{N}\,\text{bytes} / B_\text{eff}$. At 25 GB/s (single 200Gb/s link) that is `490 / 25 ≈ 19.6 s` per step ... At the H100 NVLink directional peak of 450 GB/s, the same ideal ring estimate is `490/450 ≈ 1.09 s`. The 900 GB/s bidirectional sum cannot divide a send-only traffic count
observed: The DP gradient-sync example counts 490 GB (= 2(N-1)/N × M = send + receive) and divides it by a *directional* bandwidth (450 GB/s, 25 GB/s). Ch 9 §3 Option A, for the identical eight-rank ring structure, counts 245 GB (send only) and divides by the same 450 GB/s directional peak, giving 0.54 s, and explicitly notes the equivalent form '490 GB of sent-plus-received traffic divided by 900 GB/s gives the same time'. Ch 10's own TP subsection uses the Ch 9 convention (send-only 448 KiB per call ÷ 450 GB/s). The DP subsection therefore mixes conventions within one chapter and contradicts Ch 9 by a factor of two.
evidence: Ring all-reduce, N=8: per phase each rank sends (N-1)/N × M = 122.5 GB; two phases => send total 245 GB, receive total 245 GB, total traffic 490 GB. With concurrent send/receive on separate directions, elapsed time = send volume ÷ per-direction bandwidth = 245/450 = 0.544 s (Ch 9 Option A, and the nccl-tests busbw normalization busbw = size×2(N-1)/N / time = 490/0.544 = 900 GB/s). Ch 10's 490/450 = 1.089 s double-counts the receive direction. Likewise 490/25 = 19.6 s should be 245/25 = 9.8 s. The sentence 'The 900 GB/s bidirectional sum cannot divide a send-only traffic count' shows the convention was known, yet the computation immediately above mixes send+receive with a directional denominator.
root_cause: Two incompatible definitions of 'per-rank traffic' (send-only vs send+receive) coexist in the book; the DP worked example uses the send+receive figure with a per-direction bandwidth.
correction: Restate the DP example in the Ch 9 convention: per-rank send volume = 2(N-1)/N × M = 490 GB is wrong as a 'send' figure — the send volume is 245 GB and the total (send+receive) is 490 GB. Then T_ring = 245 GB / B_dir: 245/450 ≈ 0.54 s at the H100 directional peak and 245/25 ≈ 9.8 s on a single 200 Gb/s link (or equivalently 490/900 and 490/50). Add one sentence defining 'per-rank traffic' once (send volume, receive volume, total) and reuse it in Ch 9, Ch 10 TP, Ch 10 DP, Ch 10 EP and Ch 10 FSDP. If the intent was to keep 490 GB, then the denominators must be the bidirectional figures (900 GB/s, 50 GB/s) and the printed results change accordingly.
acceptance_test: A single re-derivation script reproduces, for the same eight-rank ring and the same M, identical elapsed times in Ch 9 §3 Option A, Ch 10 TP, and Ch 10 DP; each printed time equals (send volume)/(directional bandwidth) with the direction convention stated in the same sentence.

page_hint: Ch 12, §8 End-of-Chapter Mini-Case (economics paragraph); compare Table 12-2 row 'Monthly fully loaded cost'
quoted_clause: the Ch 17 Table 17-1 provisioning policy (70% × 95% + N−1) yields 32 hosts at the same 40 rps peak (Ch 13), i.e. ~$232.2K self-host and ~$467.2K cloud-equivalent at the same per-host rates ($155,816.93, ≈$24.97/1K on the 6.24M‑req/mo business‑hours basis, Ch 16 — the cloud legs are $87,600 ≈ $14.04/1K at the default paid-occupancy input and $306,600 ≈ $49.13/1K at 21 hosts always-on)
observed: The self-host figure for 32 hosts is not the 21-host figure scaled at the same per-host rate. $155,816.93 / 21 = $7,419.85 per host per month; 32 × $7,419.85 = $237,435, not $232,200. Conversely $232,200 / 32 = $7,256.25 per host, and 21 × $7,256.25 = $152,381 ≠ $155,816.93. The cloud leg is internally consistent ($14,600/host = $20/hr × 730 hr; 21 × 14,600 = $306,600; 32 × 14,600 = $467,200), so the self-host leg is the outlier.
evidence: Recomputation: 155,816.93 ÷ 21 = 7,419.85; × 32 = 237,435.2. The printed $232.2K implies 7,256.25/host, which does not reproduce the 21-host total. The per-1K figures ($24.97, $49.13, $14.04) all reproduce correctly against the 6.24M-req/mo basis, so the error is confined to the 32-host self-host total.
root_cause: The 32-host self-host total was computed with a different per-host rate (or a different host count) than the 21-host total it is stated to scale from.
correction: Either restate the 32-host self-host total as 32 × $7,419.85 ≈ $237.4K (and update the '~10.4× over budget' ratio if it is recomputed from it: 237,435/15,000 ≈ 15.8×), or state explicitly why the per-host self-host rate differs between the 21-host and 32-host configurations (e.g. a shared-support or depreciation component) and show the derivation. Keep the cloud leg as is.
acceptance_test: One per-host monthly rate is stated once; every host-count total in Ch 12 (21, 32) and every per-1K figure reproduces from it by multiplication, with the ratio to the $15,000 budget recomputed from the same total.

page_hint: Ch 12, Table 12-1 (row (a), 'SLO' column) and §3 Candidate (a); compare Table 12-2 row 'Feasibility at declared SLO'
quoted_clause: Table 12-1: '✓ memory 164 < 640 GB · ✓ TTFT SLO (median ≤1.2 s, p95 ≤2 s)' | §3: 'per-request prefill + decode stay within the latency budget thanks to prefix caching and the high bandwidth of 8×H100' | Table 12-2: '**? unmeasured** — peak prefill and SLO not demonstrated; illustrative screen only'

Keep the memory ✓ (it is an arithmetic fact) and the quality status explicit ('reference model — gate satisfied by definition, not by measurement').

page_hint: Ch 9, §3 Worked Example Options B and C; §2 Mental Model; Fig 9.1 caption
quoted_clause: A realistic *effective* throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node — the multi-rail effective bandwidth referenced in §9.2 and Fig 9.1) ... $T_\text{ring} \approx 2\frac{N-1}{N}\frac{M}{B_\text{eff}} = 2\frac{7}{8}\frac{140 \text{ GB}}{40 \text{ GB/s}} \approx 6.1 \text{ s}$ ... a practical effective bandwidth might be 2.5 GB/s ... $\approx 98 \text{ s}$
observed: The chapter makes directionality its central rule ('The bandwidth denominator must use the same direction convention as the counted bytes'), yet the two fabric bandwidths used in the worked example are never given a direction convention. 'Aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports' reads as a bidirectional aggregate (2 × 25 GB/s = 50 GB/s per direction, 100 GB/s bidirectional), in which case 245/40 = 6.1 s double-counts the receive direction and the correct value is 490/40 = 12.25 s. If instead 40 GB/s is per-direction (2 rails × 20 GB/s effective), the printed 6.1 s is right but the phrase 'aggregated' is misleading. The same ambiguity applies to 2.5 GB/s (25 Gb/s = 3.125 GB/s per direction; 80% efficiency gives 2.5 GB/s per direction, not bidirectional).
evidence: Option A states the convention explicitly ('The corresponding peak in one direction is 450 GB/s') and uses send-volume ÷ directional bandwidth; Options B and C use the same arithmetic with an unstated convention. The 'Common Mistakes' bullet then calls both figures 'optimistic ~80% upper bounds', which is only true if they are per-direction (40/50 and 2.5/3.125).
root_cause: The direction convention was made explicit for NVLink (where a datasheet number is bidirectional) but not for the two assumed effective fabric figures, even though the chapter's own rule requires it.
correction: State the convention in the same sentence as each figure: '40 GB/s per direction (two HDR rails, ~80% of the 50 GB/s per-direction line rate)' and '2.5 GB/s per direction (25 Gb/s ≈ 3.125 GB/s per direction, ~80% after overhead)'. Then add one line: 'the ring time uses the send volume (245 GB) divided by the per-direction bandwidth; equivalently the 490 GB send+receive total divided by the bidirectional aggregate.' Repeat the convention in the Fig 9.1 caption, which currently says only '40 GB/s for an assumed effective two-rail HDR path'.
acceptance_test: Every bandwidth number that appears as a denominator in Ch 9 carries an explicit 'per direction' or 'bidirectional aggregate' qualifier in the same sentence, and the 6.1 s / 98 s / 0.54 s trio reproduces under the stated convention.

page_hint: Ch 11, §6 Architecture Consequence, subsection 'The serving concerns transfer; the text mechanisms do not transfer automatically' (four paragraphs, ~500 words)
quoted_clause: A video service still schedules requests, manages live state, reuses valid work, and chooses resource-specialized pools. The mechanisms implementing those concerns differ. The inspected full-clip Wan path does not emit a completed next frame at each denoising step.
observed: This block introduces a second workload class (video/diffusion) into a chapter whose stated job is the four serving mechanisms for the canonical text workload, and it does so after the chapter's own conclusion (the engine-capability table and the qualification gates). It is not connected to the canonical workload, to the four concerns, or to any later chapter's reasoning; it duplicates framing that Ch 14 then develops again as 'A video benchmark is a workload tuple'. The reader meets a second workload class at the very end of the serving chapter, with no bridge back to the mechanism list.
evidence: Ch 11's own Architect's Question promises 'how requests are batched, how KV cache memory is managed, how repeated prefixes are reused, and when to split prefill from decode'. The video paragraphs answer none of these for the canonical case; they answer them for diffusion models, which the chapter never introduces. Ch 14 §4 covers the same ground as a benchmark protocol.
root_cause: Material added for breadth (showing the concerns transfer) without an architectural job inside the chapter's argument; the same material is needed again in Ch 14, so it is paid for twice.
correction: Move the four video paragraphs to a single appendix (e.g. 'Appendix X — Beyond autoregressive text: video and diffusion serving'), and replace them in Ch 11 §6 with three sentences that make the transfer point explicitly: the four concerns are workload-independent, the mechanisms are not, and the canonical workload's mechanisms are the ones this chapter's arithmetic applies to. In Ch 14, keep the benchmark-protocol material and cross-reference the appendix for the serving-mechanism side. If the material stays in Ch 11, it must be moved before the engine-capability table and tied to the four concerns one by one.
acceptance_test: Ch 11 contains exactly one workload class (the canonical text workload) in its worked example and architecture consequence; any second workload class appears once, in an appendix, and is cross-referenced rather than restated.

page_hint: Ch 11, §4 Measurement, subsection 'Serving qualification: model support is not serving capability' (and the three paragraphs that follow it on adaptive depth)
quoted_clause: ### Serving qualification: model support is not serving capability ... Model support is not a complete serving capability. A hybrid model (a transformer interleaved with a recurrent/state-space block) can require both paged history and bounded recurrent state.
observed: This subsection and the three paragraphs on adaptive depth are a capability-qualification argument (what a model architecture requires of a runtime, and how to evaluate it), placed inside a section titled 'Measurement' whose other content is a numbered list of four telemetry habits. The reader looking for 'what to measure' finds instead a taxonomy of model classes and a discussion of early-exit interfaces.
evidence: §4's four numbered items are all measurement actions; the qualification subsection contains no measurement action, and its own conclusion ('A capability record can therefore identify the exact model revision, engine revision, state representation, cache policy, precision, and supported execution paths') is a record-keeping prescription that belongs with the qualification gates later in §6 ('A compact qualification record can contain seven gates').
root_cause: Section-boundary drift: a §6-grade qualification argument was placed in §4, and §6 later re-opens the same subject with a seven-gate list, so the chapter states the qualification contract twice in two different vocabularies.
correction: Move the 'Serving qualification' and adaptive-depth paragraphs into §6, immediately before the seven-gate qualification record, and merge them with it: the model-class requirements (paged history + bounded recurrent state; iteration-specific caches; early-exit runtime path) become the first gate ('the model revision's execution path is supported end-to-end'), and the adaptive-depth paragraphs become the note on why per-token depth changes the scheduler's unit of work. §4 then keeps only the four telemetry habits plus one added item: 'record the model revision and the execution path in use, so a fallback (e.g. SDPA instead of paged attention) is visible in telemetry'.
acceptance_test: §4 contains only measurement actions; the qualification contract appears once in the chapter, in §6, with one vocabulary; the seven gates include the model-class requirements.

page_hint: Ch 9, §8 End-of-Chapter Mini-Case (paragraph on tensor parallelism)
quoted_clause: for the canonical 8×H100 host the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations (tens of MBs, not GBs, at the canonical batch and hidden size — it scales with batch × hidden width per layer)
observed: The parenthetical attaches 'tens of MBs' to the per-layer exchange, but at the canonical batch and hidden width the per-layer exchange is ~0.25 MB logical / ~0.44 MB sent per rank (Ch 10's worked example: M = 16 × 8,192 × 2 = 256 KiB; ring send 448 KiB per call). 'Tens of MBs' is the per-decode-step total across 80 layers (70 MiB), not the per-layer figure. As written, a reader could conclude that each layer's collective moves tens of megabytes, which would change the latency conclusion by two orders of magnitude.
evidence: Ch 10 §3: 'Across 160 calls (two per block × 80 blocks), each rank sends 70 MiB and receives 70 MiB in that one decode step.' Per call: 448 KiB sent. So the correct statement is 'hundreds of KB per layer, tens of MB per decode step'.
root_cause: The per-layer and per-step scales were conflated when the sentence was written; the parenthetical's own qualifier ('scales with batch × hidden width per layer') points at the per-layer quantity.
correction: Rewrite as: 'the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations — at the canonical batch and hidden width, ~0.25 MB logical per collective and ~0.45 MB sent per rank per call, i.e. tens of MB per decode step across 80 layers (Ch 10), not GBs.'
acceptance_test: The mini-case's per-layer and per-step byte figures match the Ch 10 worked example exactly, and the reader can tell which scale 'tens of MBs' refers to.

page_hint: Ch 9, §5 Common Mistakes, bullet 'Overlooking protocol overhead'
quoted_clause: 200/400GbE transcodes 64b/66b to 256b/257b before FEC; InfiniBand coding varies by generation ... An NDR 400 Gb/s InfiniBand link delivers a ~380 Gb/s class useful payload; a 200 Gb/s RoCEv2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s.
observed: The 256b/257b block-coding layer belongs to 400G/800G multi-lane Ethernet (IEEE 802.3ck); 200GbE Ethernet is two 100G lanes using 64b/66b plus FEC, with no 256b/257b stage. The sentence as written attributes 256b/257b to 200GbE as well. The payload-efficiency numbers themselves are defensible (400 × 64/66 = 388 Gb/s; 200 × 64/66 = 194 Gb/s before framing/FEC).
evidence: IEEE 802.3ck defines 256b/257b for 400G/800G; 200GbE (802.3cd) uses 64b/66b with RS-FEC on two lanes. The book's own derived figures (≈380 Gb/s for NDR, ≈180 Gb/s for 200GbE RoCEv2) are consistent with 64b/66b plus framing/FEC, not with an additional 256b/257b stage.
root_cause: The line-coding description was written for the 400G case and generalized to 200G without checking the standard.
correction: Rewrite as: 'Ethernet line coding differs by generation: 200GbE uses 64b/66b with FEC on two 100G lanes, while 400GbE adds a 256b/257b block-coding stage before FEC; InfiniBand HDR and NDR both use 64b/66b. Use the specific standard's payload-efficiency figure.'
acceptance_test: The line-coding description names the standard and generation for each rate quoted, and the derived payload figures (≈380 Gb/s NDR, ≈180 Gb/s 200GbE) reproduce from the stated coding.

page_hint: Ch 12, §3 Worked Example, Candidate (a) closing sentences
quoted_clause: Quality: the 70B is itself the workload's quality reference, so this gate is met by construction.
observed: 'Met by construction' overstates what is known. The 70B is the reference model, so candidate (a) inherits the reference's quality by definition — but the workload's quality requirement ('must achieve ~70B-model answer quality on enterprise prompts', §8) is a statement about the deployed system on the true evaluation set, which no measurement in the book establishes. The same chapter treats quality as an empirical gate for candidate (c) and as an open question in §7.
evidence: Ch 12 §3 candidate (c): 'Whether a 7B-class model can match the 70B model's answer quality on this workload is not derivable from parameter count ... It is an empirical question answered only by running the actual evaluation set.' Ch 14 §1 makes capability benchmarking the screen that 'picks which models qualify'.
root_cause: The gate was scored by reference identity rather than by the gate's own criterion (evaluation-set result), and the two framings were not reconciled.
correction: Rewrite as: 'Quality: the 70B is the workload's quality reference, so candidate (a) inherits the reference quality by definition rather than by measurement — the gate is satisfied relative to the reference, and the absolute requirement still needs the Ch 14 capability screen on the true evaluation set.'
acceptance_test: The quality status of candidates (a) and (b) is stated in the same terms as candidate (c)'s (reference-relative vs measured), and no candidate is described as having 'met' a quality gate without an evaluation-set result.

quoted_clause: Ch 11 §2: 'Serving is managing three precious resources against a stream of arrivals: GPU compute (FLOPs, bound in prefill), GPU memory bandwidth (HBM, bound in decode), and GPU memory capacity (HBM bytes, bound by KV cache).' | Ch 12 §2: 'compute (prefill throughput — prefill is compute-bound, Ch 11, scoped to the canonical architecture × batch × precision × kernel operating point), memory bandwidth (decode throughput — decode is bandwidth-bound)'

page_hint: Ch 17 §4, bullet 'The 25 ms/token in W is the TPOT budget, not a measured per-step time'; also Ch 15 §3 'Compute demand versus peak' and Ch 17 §4 'Simultaneous feasibility check'
quoted_clause: The decode-bandwidth floor for the canonical 8×H100 host is 140 GB ÷ (8 × 3.35 TB/s) ≈ 5.2 ms/step, so a well-tuned decode can run well under the 25 ms SLO.
observed: The 5.2 ms/step floor counts only weight traffic. It omits the per-step KV read traffic, which at the canonical geometry is the larger term: every decode step must read the full KV of every resident sequence (24.9037 GB per 9,500-token request), so at the canonical occupancy of 17 resident requests a step reads 140 GB (weights) + 17 × 24.9037 GB (KV) ≈ 563.4 GB, i.e. ≈21.0 ms/step at 26.8 TB/s — about 4x the printed floor. The inference 'a well-tuned decode can run well under the 25 ms SLO' therefore does not follow at the canonical context length and concurrency. The same omission makes the decode leg's feasibility at the canonical peak invisible: 12,000 output tok/s x (140/B + 24.1) GB/token ≈ 388 TB/s at B = 17, roughly 14x the host's HBM bandwidth.
evidence: Recomputed: 140 GB + 17 x 24.9037 GB = 563.4 GB; 563.4 GB / (8 x 3.35 TB/s = 26.8 TB/s) = 21.0 ms/step. Ch 15 §1 itself names 'the memory traffic of KV cache reads and writes on every token step' as a dominant cost, so the term is in the book's own vocabulary but never quantified.
root_cause: The decode-bandwidth model was built from the weight-stream term only; the KV-read term was never quantified, so the canonical service time W = 8.6 s, the in-flight count 344, and the 21/31/32-host fleet counts all rest on an unquantified term.
